e-459.knowledge_point: Integrating the Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent
e-459.worked_solution:
If we let $u=1-3x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = -\dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{1-3x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{1-3x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

e-460.knowledge_point: Integrating a General Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent
e-460.worked_solution:
If we let $u=5+4x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 4 \textrm d u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {3}^{5+4x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {3}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {3}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{3}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{3}^{5+4x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{x/2\,-\,1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\,{e}^{u}+C \\  & =2\,{e}^{x/2\,-\,1}+C\end{aligned}
$$

If we let $u=\frac{x}{2}-1,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,2\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{x/2\,-\,1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\,{e}^{u}+C \\  & =2\,{e}^{x/2\,-\,1}+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
First, we notice that

$$
\int {e}^{z}{e}^{z}\,\text{d}z=\int {e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z.
$$

If we let $u=2z$, then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}z=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z & =\int {e}^{2z}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2z}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2z}}{2}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |

$$

$$

after.worked_solution:
If we let $u=\frac{x}{3},$ then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\text{d}u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {6}^{x/3}\,\text{d}x & =\int {6}^{u}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int {6}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\frac{{6}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C \\  & =\frac{3\cdot {6}^{x/3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C\end{aligned}
$$
